study.title: Exodus 7 The authority of God before Pharaoh and the beginning of the judgments
study.overview: Exodus 7 shows God by reaffirming the mission of Moses and Aaron, preparing them to face Pharaoh and demonstrating that the deliverance of Israel would not depend on human eloquence, but on the power of the LORD. The chapter advances in two decisive signs: the staff of Aaron turned into a snake, which is imitated by the Egyptian magicians but overcome by the superiority of the sign of God; and the first plague, when the waters of Egypt become blood. In the whole chapter, Pharaoh resists, and this resistance ends up serving to multiply the divine signs and reveal to the Egyptians that the Lord is the true God.

outline.title: Reinforced commission and sending before Pharaoh
outline.explanation: God appoints Moses as his representative before Pharaoh and Aaron as a spokesman. The LORD also announces beforehand that Pharaoh will resist, but that this resistance will not thwart the divine plan. Moses and Aaron obey, even though they are already elderly men, which emphasizes that the effectiveness of the mission comes from God, not from their natural strength.

outline.title: The first sign: the staff becomes snake
outline.explanation: When Pharaoh demands a miracle, God sends Aaron to throw the rod to the ground. The sign authenticates the message, but the wise and enchanters of Egypt also produce something similar. Still, Aaron's rod devours others, showing the superiority of the power of the LORD. But Pharaoh hardens his heart and hears not.

outline.title: The first plague: the river becomes blood
outline.explanation: God commands Moses to confront Pharaoh by the river and to announce the first great plague. All the waters of Egypt are struck, the fish die, the river becomes unfit to drink, and the Egyptians seek wells around the river. Even so, the magicians make a partial imitation, and Pharaoh remains stubborn. The chapter ends by highlighting that the plague lasted seven days.

study.context: The chapter takes place in the context of the confrontation between the God of Israel and the King of Egypt. The text presents Moses and Aaron going to speak to Pharaoh in the name of the LORD, after God had prepared his vocation and promised signs. The chapter itself informs that Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three, showing that the mission begins late according to human criteria, but at the right time of God. It is not necessary to resort to external reconstructions to realize the scenario: it is a dispute of authority between the most powerful king of Egypt and the God who demands the liberation of his people.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God rules history by his word and by his powerful acts. Moses is called in a special way to represent God before Pharaoh, which underlines delegated authority, not essential divinity. Aaron acts as a spokesperson, and this shows that God uses human mediations without relying on them. The hardening of Pharaoh's heart appears as judgment and as part of God's purpose to manifest his signs. Theologically, the text insists that the LORD wants to be known: by the Israelites, the Egyptians and by Pharaoh himself. The signs are not empty spectacle; they are confirmation of the word and announcement of judgment. The imitation of the magicians reveals that similar signs do not guarantee truth, and the superiority of the divine sign is seen when Aaron's rod devours others. The plague of the waters in blood reaches a central source of life and sustenance, showing that the LORD has power over creation and on what the Egyptians trusted. The chapter also anticipates a recurring theme in Exodus: human resistance does not prevent God's faithfulness, but ends up serving the purpose of revealing his glory.

scholarViews.insight: The comment points out that the decisive factor is not the eloquence of Moses, but the power of God; Moses obeys and acts, while Pharaoh refuses to hear.
The commentary sees confrontation as a dispute between the power of God and that of a proud prince, in which God will certainly prevail.
The commentary states that Pharaoh's heart hardening is presented as divine permission for God to multiply his wonders and the Egyptians know that the LORD is the only God.

questions: What does this chapter reveal about the difference between human authority and God's authority?
Why did not Pharaoh's signs lead to repentance, and what does this teach about the hardness of the human heart?
How can the repetition of signs and judgments strengthen the faith of God's people even when the wicked remains resistant?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to obey God even when the initial answer seems negative. It also invites us to trust that the word of the LORD has more weight than the resistance of powerful people. In practice, this means persevering in obedience, speaking faithfully when God sends us and not measuring the truth by immediate success. In facing opposition, the believer must remember that God continues to act, even if the human heart proves to be stubborn. The concrete application is to examine where we are hardened to God's voice and ask Him to make us sensitive to his word, rather than imitating Pharaoh in his refusal.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not definitively clarify the exact nature of the snake of the signal or the precise form of the action of the magicians; therefore, these questions should be treated with caution. It is also not possible to affirm, based only on this material, additional historical details about the identity of the magicians, the exact chronology of pests or the broad political context beyond what the chapter itself informs.
